claim: ztf-11 is the sole Caenorhabditis elegans Myt1 homolog.
source: Here, we show that ztf-11 (Zinc-finger Transcription Factor-11), the sole Caenorhabditis elegans Myt1 homolog, is required for neurogenesis in multiple neuronal lineages from previously differentiated epithelial cells, including a neuron generated by a developmental epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation event.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of ztf-11.

claim: ztf-11 is required for neurogenesis in multiple neuronal lineages from previously differentiated epithelial cells.
source: Here, we show that ztf-11 (Zinc-finger Transcription Factor-11), the sole Caenorhabditis elegans Myt1 homolog, is required for neurogenesis in multiple neuronal lineages from previously differentiated epithelial cells, including a neuron generated by a developmental epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation event.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: ztf-11 is required for a neuron generated by a developmental epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation event.
source: Here, we show that ztf-11 (Zinc-finger Transcription Factor-11), the sole Caenorhabditis elegans Myt1 homolog, is required for neurogenesis in multiple neuronal lineages from previously differentiated epithelial cells, including a neuron generated by a developmental epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation event.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data on Y-to-PDA transdifferentiation.

claim: ztf-11 is exclusively expressed in all neuronal precursors with remarkable specificity at single-cell resolution.
source: ztf-11 is exclusively expressed in all neuronal precursors with remarkable specificity at single-cell resolution.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by lineage tracing data showing 87% of neuronal precursors express ZTF-11 while only 7% of non-neuronal precursors do.

claim: Loss of ztf-11 leads to upregulation of non-neuronal genes.
source: Loss of ztf-11 leads to upregulation of non-neuronal genes and reduced neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq data showing 88% of differentially expressed genes were upregulated in ztf-11 knockdown.

claim: Loss of ztf-11 leads to reduced neurogenesis.
source: Loss of ztf-11 leads to upregulation of non-neuronal genes and reduced neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data showing loss of neuronal markers in multiple lineages.

claim: Ectopic expression of ztf-11 in epidermal lineages is sufficient to produce additional neurons.
source: Ectopic expression of ztf-11 in epidermal lineages is sufficient to produce additional neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data showing ectopic PVD-like cells in 45% of transgenic animals expressing ZTF-11 in seam cells.

claim: ZTF-11 functions together with the MuvB corepressor complex to suppress the activation of non-neuronal genes in neurons.
source: ZTF-11 functions together with the MuvB corepressor complex to suppress the activation of non-neuronal genes in neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic analysis and SiMPull experiments showing direct binding between ZTF-11 and MuvB components.

claim: Myt1 family proteins counteract lateral inhibition and subsequently commit neuronal progenitors to terminal differentiation.
source: Based on these results, it has been proposed that Myt1 family proteins counteract lateral inhibition and subsequently commit neuronal progenitors to terminal differentiation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on previous research cited in the introduction.

claim: Myt1l, together with the proneural gene Ascl1 and the neuronal transcription factor Brn2, are sufficient to induce transdifferentiation into neurons from various cell types.
source: Recent in vitro studies showed that Myt1l, together with the proneural gene Ascl1 and the neuronal transcription factor Brn2, are sufficient to induce transdifferentiation (TD) into neurons from various cell types (Masserdotti et al., 2016; Vierbuchen et al., 2010; Wapinski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: Non-neuronal mouse embryonic fibroblast signature genes were repressed by Myt1l during neuronal transdifferentiation.
source: Interestingly, a number of non-neuronal mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) signature genes were also found to be repressed by Myt1l during neuronal transdifferentiation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Co-expression of Myt1l reduced efficiency of MyoD-induced myocyte differentiation in vitro.
source: Furthermore, co-expression of Myt1l reduced efficiency of MyoD-induced myocyte differentiation in vitro (Mall et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Myt1l was found to be associated with transcriptional corepressor complexes, including the Sin3 histone deacetylase complex (Sin3-HDAC), to mediate repression of non-neuronal genes.
source: Consistent with a role for Mytl1 in transcriptional repression during neuronal transdifferentiation, Myt1l was found to be associated with transcriptional corepressor complexes, including the Sin3 histone deacetylase complex (Sin3-HDAC), to mediate repression of non-neuronal genes (Romm et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Redundancy between Myt1 family proteins has prevented mouse models from providing insight into the developmental functions of Myt1.
source: Redundancy between Myt1 family proteins has prevented mouse models from providing insight into the developmental functions of Myt1 (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The DNA-binding zinc finger domains of ZTF-11 exhibit a high degree of conservation in amino acid sequence compared to other Myt1 family members.
source: The DNA-binding zinc finger domains of ZTF-11 exhibit a high degree of conservation in amino acid sequence compared to other Myt1 family members (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing amino acid alignment.

claim: Both ZTF-11 and vertebrate Myt1 family proteins recognize the same consensus sequence (AAGTT) in vitro.
source: Both ZTF-11 and vertebrate Myt1 family proteins recognize the same consensus sequence (AAGTT) in vitro (Mall et al., 2017; Narasimhan et al., 2015; Vasconcelos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Apart from the zinc finger domains, ZTF-11 and other Myt1 family proteins are poorly conserved in sequence, including regions that interact with the Sin-3-HDAC complex.
source: Apart from the zinc finger domains, ZTF-11 and other Myt1 family proteins are poorly conserved in sequence, including regions that interact with the Sin-3-HDAC complex (Mall et al., 2017; Romm et al., 2005) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ZTF-11 is required for epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation during C. elegans development.
source: Remarkably, ZTF-11 is required for epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation during C. elegans development, suggesting that in vivo transdifferentiation utilizes genetic programs similar to those required for neuronal reprogramming in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data on Y-to-PDA transdifferentiation.

claim: In vivo transdifferentiation utilizes genetic programs similar to those required for neuronal reprogramming in vitro.
source: Remarkably, ZTF-11 is required for epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation during C. elegans development, suggesting that in vivo transdifferentiation utilizes genetic programs similar to those required for neuronal reprogramming in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that ZTF-11 is required for transdifferentiation in vivo, similar to Myt1l's role in vitro.

claim: ZTF-11 is necessary and sufficient for postembryonic neurogenesis from a non-neuronal precursor.
source: We also found that ZTF-11 is necessary and sufficient for postembryonic neurogenesis from a non-neuronal precursor.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments in the V5 lineage.

claim: ztf-11 represses expression of non-neuronal genes to allow establishment of neuronal identity.
source: In these lineages, we show that ztf-11 represses expression of non-neuronal genes to allow establishment of neuronal identity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq data and genetic analysis showing retention of epithelial markers in ztf-11 mutants.

claim: ztf-11 does not function as a repressor of the Hes1 ortholog lin-22 in the context of postembryonic neurogenesis.
source: Unexpectedly, ztf-11 does not function as a repressor of the Hes1 ortholog lin-22 in this context.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genetic analysis and expression data showing no change in lin-22 expression in ztf-11 mutants.

claim: ZTF-11 acts downstream of Hes1 to promote neuronal differentiation.
source: Instead, our genetic data support the model that ZTF-11 acts downstream of Hes1 to promote neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference supported by genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: ZTF-11 mediates transcriptional repression through directly binding to MuvB co-repressor complex, but not the Sin3-HDAC complex.
source: We further show that ZTF-11 mediates transcriptional repression through directly binding to MuvB co-repressor complex, but not the Sin3-HDAC complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genetic analysis and SiMPull experiments showing direct binding.

claim: Neurogenesis requires repression of non-neuronal programs by Myt1 family proteins in addition to activation of neuronal programs.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that neurogenesis requires repression of non-neuronal programs by Myt1 family proteins in addition to activation of neuronal programs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings of the study.

claim: Insertion of GFP and loxP sites in the ztf-11 locus did not yield any overt phenotypes.
source: Insertion of GFP and loxP sites in the ztf-11 locus did not yield any overt phenotypes.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental manipulation of the ztf-11 locus.

claim: A deletion spanning one of two zinc-finger domains (tm2315) was homozygous lethal and produced severely paralyzed, developmentally arrested L1 larvae when maintained with the hT2 balancer chromosome.
source: In comparison, a deletion spanning one of two zinc-finger domains (tm2315), which likely abolished DNA binding, was homozygous lethal and produced severely paralyzed, developmentally arrested L1 larvae when maintained with the hT2 balancer chromosome (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental analysis of the tm2315 deletion mutant.

claim: ZTF-11::GFP fluorescence was predominantly localized to nuclei.
source: As expected, we found that ZTF-11::GFP fluorescence was predominantly localized to nuclei (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ZTF-11::GFP is expressed in neural precursors starting in the mid-gastrula embryo (~100-cell stage).
source: As with vertebrate orthologs, we found that ZTF-11::GFP is expressed in neural precursors starting in the mid-gastrula embryo (~100-cell stage) (Figure 1B and Video 1).
evidence: This is an observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: ZTF-11::GFP expression was strongest during the late gastrula to lima-bean embryonic stages, coinciding with the birth of most embryonically generated neurons.
source: ZTF-11::GFP expression was strongest during the late gastrula to lima-bean embryonic stages, coinciding with the birth of most embryonically generated neurons.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: ZTF-11::GFP expression became weaker in subsequent stages of embryogenesis.
source: ZTF-11::GFP expression became weaker in subsequent stages of embryogenesis.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: Around the time of hatching, ZTF-11::GFP could only be detected in a small number of neuronal nuclei.
source: Around the time of hatching, ZTF-11::GFP could only be detected in a small number of neuronal nuclei.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: Post-embryonic ZTF-11::GFP expression was transiently observed in postembryonic neuroectoblasts, such as Pn, Q, and V5 cells, but was quickly extinguished in postmitotic neurons.
source: Post-embryonic ZTF-11::GFP expression showed a similar pattern; ZTF-11::GFP expression was transiently observed in postembryonic neuroectoblasts, such as Pn, Q, and V5 cells, but was quickly extinguished in postmitotic neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: ZTF-11 is transiently expressed in neuronal precursors and postmitotic neurons.
source: Together, these data suggest that ZTF-11 is transiently expressed in neuronal precursors and postmitotic neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the expression pattern observations.

claim: At the 350-cell stage, 126 of 145 (87%) neuronal precursor cells expressed ZTF-11::GFP.
source: At the 350-cell stage, 126 of 145 (87%) neuronal precursor cells expressed ZTF-11::GFP.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: All six neuroectoblasts (P7/8, P5/6, and P3/4) that did not express ZTF-11 at the 350-cell stage showed postembryonic expression of ZTF-11.
source: All six neuroectoblasts (P7/8, P5/6, and P3/4) that did not express ZTF-11 at the 350-cell stage showed postembryonic expression of ZTF-11.
evidence: This is an observation from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Only 15 of 195 (7%) non-neuronal precursor cells expressed ZTF-11::GFP.
source: In contrast, only 15 of 195 (7%) non-neuronal precursor cells expressed ZTF-11::GFP.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Strong correlations between ztf-11 expression and neuronal cell fate were evident in all branches of the lineages at single-cell resolution.
source: Strong correlations between ztf-11 expression and neuronal cell fate were evident in all branches of the lineages at single-cell resolution (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an observation supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ZTF-11 plays a broad role in neurogenesis.
source: These observations suggest that ZTF-11 plays a broad role in neurogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the widespread expression of ZTF-11 in neuronal precursors.

claim: The expression pattern of the Myt1 family proteins closely follows proneural bHLH genes in vertebrate systems.
source: The expression pattern of the Myt1 family proteins closely follows proneural bHLH (basic helix-loop-helix) genes in vertebrate systems (Bellefroid et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The vertebrate Myt1 family proteins are direct transcriptional targets of proneural genes, including Ascl1.
source: The vertebrate Myt1 family proteins are direct transcriptional targets of proneural genes, including Ascl1 (Mall et al., 2017; Vasconcelos et al., 2016; Wapinski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: C. elegans proneural genes are conserved through evolution and act as master regulators of neurogenesis.
source: C. elegans proneural genes are conserved through evolution and act as master regulators of neurogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans proneural genes.

claim: C. elegans proneural genes are expressed in neuronal precursors and differentiating neurons.
source: These proneural genes are expressed in neuronal precursors and differentiating neurons (Frank et al., 2003; Hallam et al., 2000; Murray et al., 2012; Zhao and Emmons, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: All C. elegans proneural genes, including HLH-3/Achaete-Scute, LIN-32/Atonal, NGN-1/neurogenin, and CND-1/NeuroD, form heterodimers with HLH-2/Daughterless and bind to canonical E-boxes (CANNTG) to regulate transcription of target genes.
source: All C. elegans proneural genes, including HLH-3/Achaete-Scute, LIN-32/Atonal, NGN-1/neurogenin, and CND-1/NeuroD, form heterodimers with HLH-2/Daughterless and bind to canonical E-boxes (CANNTG) to regulate transcription of target genes (Grove et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Hypomorphic hlh-2(tm1768) mutant showed a strong reduction of ztf-11 transcriptional reporter signal (78%) in comparison to wild type.
source: We found that hypomorphic hlh-2(tm1768) mutant showed a strong reduction of ztf-11 transcriptional reporter signal (78%) in comparison to wild type (Figure 2A), suggesting that hlh-2 is required for proper expression of ztf-11.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from reporter expression experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: hlh-2 is required for proper expression of ztf-11.
source: We found that hypomorphic hlh-2(tm1768) mutant showed a strong reduction of ztf-11 transcriptional reporter signal (78%) in comparison to wild type (Figure 2A), suggesting that hlh-2 is required for proper expression of ztf-11.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reporter expression data.

claim: The proneural dimer partners of HLH-2 are redundantly expressed at early stages of neuronal development.
source: In contrast to the essential hlh-2, the proneural dimer partners of HLH-2 are redundantly expressed at early stages of neuronal development (Grove et al., 2009; Murray et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Endogenous ZTF-11::GFP expression was largely unperturbed in single mutants of hlh-3(ot354), cnd-1(ju29) or ngn-1(ok2200).
source: Consistent with this redundancy, endogenous ZTF-11::GFP expression was largely unperturbed in single mutants of hlh-3(ot354), cnd-1(ju29) or ngn-1(ok2200) (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from expression analysis in mutant backgrounds.

claim: lin-32(n372) mutant showed loss of ZTF-11 expression in the postembryonic postdeirid lineage, where LIN-32 functions to generate sensory neurons.
source: We found that lin-32(n372) mutant showed loss of ZTF-11 expression in the postembryonic postdeirid lineage, where LIN-32 functions to generate sensory neurons (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is an observation from expression analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Mutating E-box sequences (CANNTG to ACNNAG) (∆E-box) caused a severe reduction (79%) of ∆E-box reporter signal compared to wild-type reporter.
source: Mutating these E-box sequences (CANNTG to ACNNAG) (∆E-box) caused a severe reduction (79%) of ∆E-box reporter signal compared to wild-type reporter (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from reporter expression experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Proneural genes and HLH-2 together activate the expression of ztf-11 in neuronal precursors through the E-boxes in the ztf-11 promoter.
source: These results are consistent with findings in vertebrates and suggest that proneural genes and HLH-2 together activate the expression of ztf-11 in neuronal precursors through the E-boxes in the ztf-11 promoter.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the E-box mutation and hlh-2 mutant data.

claim: An epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation event occurs invariantly during normal C. elegans development.
source: An epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation event occurs invariantly during normal C. elegans development (Jarriault et al., 2008), providing a model for investigating genetic pathways involved in neuronal transdifferentiation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The rectal epithelial Y cell undergoes an epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation event to form the motor neuron PDA in a stepwise process; epithelial identity is first lost and neuronal identity is subsequently acquired.
source: The rectal epithelial Y cell undergoes an epithelial-to-neuronal transdifferentiation event to form the motor neuron PDA in a stepwise process; epithelial identity is first lost and neuronal identity is subsequently acquired (Jarriault et al., 2008; White et al., 1986) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: At the L1 stage, the Y cell is part of the rectal epithelium.
source: At the L1 stage, the Y cell is part of the rectal epithelium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Y cell development.

claim: During the L2 stage, the Y cell gradually loses its epithelial fate (Y.0) while migrating anteriorly and gaining neuronal markers (Y.1).
source: During the L2 stage, the Y cell gradually loses its epithelial fate (Y.0) while migrating anteriorly and gaining neuronal markers (Y.1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Y cell development.

claim: In the L3 stage, the Y cell becomes the PDA neuron and extends an axon while the P12.pa cell replaces the Y cell in the anal epithelium.
source: In the L3 stage, the Y cell becomes the PDA neuron and extends an axon while the P12.pa cell replaces the Y cell in the anal epithelium (Jarriault et al., 2008; Sulston and Horvitz, 1977; White et al., 1986) (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figures 3A-B.

claim: ztf-11 was expressed in the Y cell in early L2 animals at the start of the transdifferentiation process.
source: Using the endogenously-tagged ZTF-11::GFP, we found that ztf-11 was expressed in the Y cell in early L2 animals at the start of the transdifferentiation process (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ZTF-11 expression coincided with the initial withdrawal of the Y cell from the rectum.
source: ZTF-11 expression coincided with the initial withdrawal of the Y cell from the rectum, suggesting that ZTF-11 may mediate the early dedifferentiation step of transdifferentiation (Y.0).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: ZTF-11 may mediate the early dedifferentiation step of transdifferentiation (Y.0).
source: ZTF-11 expression coincided with the initial withdrawal of the Y cell from the rectum, suggesting that ZTF-11 may mediate the early dedifferentiation step of transdifferentiation (Y.0).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the timing of ZTF-11 expression.

claim: Conditional deletion of ztf-11 in the Y cell led to the loss of PDA neuronal markers, including EXP-1 and COG-1.
source: Conditional deletion of ztf-11 in the Y cell led to the loss of PDA neuronal markers, including EXP-1 and COG-1, suggesting that PDA was not generated (Figure 3D,F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from conditional knockout experiments shown in Figures 3D, F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PDA was not generated in ztf-11 conditional knockout animals.
source: Conditional deletion of ztf-11 in the Y cell led to the loss of PDA neuronal markers, including EXP-1 and COG-1, suggesting that PDA was not generated (Figure 3D,F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the loss of PDA markers.

claim: Epithelial markers in the Y cell (EGL-26 and COL-34) persisted throughout development in ztf-11 cKO animals.
source: We found that epithelial markers in the Y cell (EGL-26 and COL-34) persisted throughout development in ztf-11 cKO animals (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The persistent Y cell in ztf-11 cKO animals retained its original rectal niche location and morphology during development.
source: Moreover, the persistent Y cell in ztf-11 cKO animals retained its original rectal niche location and morphology during development (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data shown in Figures 3E-F.

claim: ztf-11 functions to eliminate epithelial identity in the Y cell and allows for subsequent acquisition of neuronal PDA identity.
source: These results argue that ztf-11 functions to eliminate epithelial identity in the Y cell and allows for subsequent acquisition of neuronal PDA identity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the persistence of epithelial markers and loss of neuronal markers in ztf-11 cKO.

claim: Myt1l's function in in vitro neuronal transdifferentiation is in accordance with ztf-11's function in vivo.
source: This results are in accordance with Myt1l's function in in vitro neuronal transdifferentiation (Mall et al., 2017; Vierbuchen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between the current findings and previous research.

claim: Myt1 family factors may function as key evolutionarily conserved repressive factors in transdifferentiation events.
source: While mammalian models of in vivo neuronal transdifferentiation have not yet been described, Myt1 family factors may function as key evolutionarily conserved repressive factors in transdifferentiation events.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in C. elegans and previous in vitro studies.

claim: The C. elegans postdeirid is a simple sensory organ comprised of two morphologically and functionally distinct sensory neurons, PVD and PDE, and a pair of sheath (PDEsh) and socket (PDEso) glia that support the PDE sensory dendrite.
source: The C. elegans postdeirid is a simple sensory organ comprised of two morphologically and functionally distinct sensory neurons, PVD and PDE, and a pair of sheath (PDEsh) and socket (PDEso) glia that support the PDE sensory dendrite (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the postdeirid sensory organ.

claim: These four cells are born postembryonically from the V5 seam cell, which forms part of the lateral epidermis.
source: These four cells are born postembryonically from the V5 seam cell, which forms part of the lateral epidermis (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about postdeirid development.

claim: Parallel lateral epidermal seam cells of V lineages (V1-4 and V6) do not give rise to any neural progeny.
source: Unlike V5 or tail T lineages, parallel lateral epidermal seam cells of V lineages (V1-4 and V6) do not give rise to any neural progeny (Sulston and Horvitz, 1977).
evidence: This is established knowledge about V lineage development.

claim: Mutations in lin-32 cause the V5 lineage to lose postdeirid neuroblast cell fate and instead to adopt a V1-4-like cell fate.
source: Previous genetic studies have identified mutations in lin-32, the homolog of Drosophila atonal and mammalian Atoh1, which cause the V5 lineage to lose postdeirid neuroblast cell fate and instead to adopt a V1-4-like cell fate, establishing LIN-32 as the master regulator of postdeirid development (Kenyon, 1986; Zhao and Emmons, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: LIN-32 is the master regulator of postdeirid development.
source: Previous genetic studies have identified mutations in lin-32, the homolog of Drosophila atonal and mammalian Atoh1, which cause the V5 lineage to lose postdeirid neuroblast cell fate and instead to adopt a V1-4-like cell fate, establishing LIN-32 as the master regulator of postdeirid development (Kenyon, 1986; Zhao and Emmons, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Homologs of the atonal family of proneural bHLH factors function in the development of various mechanosensory modalities, including mammalian inner ear hair cells, Drosophila chordotonal organs, and the C. elegans postdeirid and male sensory rays.
source: It is interesting to note that homologs of the atonal family of proneural bHLH factors function in the development of various mechanosensory modalities, including mammalian inner ear hair cells (Bermingham et al., 1999), Drosophila chordotonal organs (Jarman et al., 1993), and the C. elegans postdeirid and male sensory rays (Zhao and Emmons, 1995), suggesting that atonal family bHLH genes drive a conserved genetic program.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Atonal family bHLH genes drive a conserved genetic program.
source: It is interesting to note that homologs of the atonal family of proneural bHLH factors function in the development of various mechanosensory modalities, including mammalian inner ear hair cells (Bermingham et al., 1999), Drosophila chordotonal organs (Jarman et al., 1993), and the C. elegans postdeirid and male sensory rays (Zhao and Emmons, 1995), suggesting that atonal family bHLH genes drive a conserved genetic program.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the conservation of atonal family function across species.

claim: ZTF-11::GFP was observed in the posterior daughter cell of V5, which gives rise to the neurons, but not in V1-4 nor in the anterior daughter of V5, which generate epidermal cells (hyp7) and seam cells.
source: Starting from mid L1, ZTF-11::GFP was observed in the posterior daughter cell of V5, which gives rise to the neurons, but not in V1-4 nor in the anterior daughter of V5, which generate epidermal cells (hyp7) and seam cells.
evidence: This is an observation from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Within the V5 lineage, ZTF-11::GFP was maintained in neurons and glia but turned off in the non-neuronal precursors.
source: Within the V5 lineage, ZTF-11::GFP was maintained in neurons and glia but turned off in the non-neuronal precursors (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from lineage tracing experiments shown in Figures 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: lin-32 expression was detected prior to expression of ZTF-11::GFP.
source: lin-32 expression was detected prior to expression of ZTF-11::GFP.
evidence: This is an observation from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: lin-32 could not be detected in late L1, while ZTF-11 expression was maintained throughout.
source: However, lin-32 could not be detected in late L1, while ZTF-11 expression was maintained throughout.
evidence: This is an observation from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: lin-32 reappeared again in the postdeirid neuroblast V5.pa, but not in epithelial sister V5.pp.
source: lin-32 reappeared again in the postdeirid neuroblast V5.pa, but not in epithelial sister V5.pp (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both LIN-32 and subsequent ZTF-11 expression were correlated with neuronal and glial cell fate.
source: While the significance of the lin-32 expression dynamics remains unclear, both LIN-32 and subsequent ZTF-11 expression were correlated with neuronal and glial cell fate.
evidence: This is an observation from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Near complete loss of ZTF-11::GFP expression was found in 70% of cKO animals.
source: We found near complete loss of ZTF-11::GFP expression in 70% of cKO animals.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from conditional knockout efficiency analysis.

claim: 30% of cKO animals showed only partial knock-down that fell within the wild type range of ZTF-11 expression, likely due to perdurance of ztf-11 mRNA or protein.
source: However, 30% of cKO animals showed only partial knock-down that fell within the wild type range of ZTF-11 expression, likely due to perdurance of ztf-11 mRNA or protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an observation from conditional knockout efficiency analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Approximately 50% of PVD and PDE neurons had lost their neuronal fate in ztf-11 cKO animals, as reflected by loss of the respective cell-type-specific markers, ser-2 and dat-1, as well as loss of the pan-neuronal rab-3 marker.
source: We found that approximately 50% of PVD and PDE neurons had lost their neuronal fate, as reflected by loss of the respective cell-type-specific markers, ser-2 and dat-1, as well as loss of the pan-neuronal rab-3 marker (Figure 4C and E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 4C, E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: A similar loss of glial markers from the socket and sheath glia that function with the PDE neuron was found in ztf-11 cKO animals.
source: Additionally, we found a similar loss of glial markers from the socket and sheath glia that function with the PDE neuron (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that ZTF-11 is also required for glial fate in the postdeirid lineage.
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ZTF-11 is also required for glial fate in the postdeirid lineage.
source: Additionally, we found a similar loss of glial markers from the socket and sheath glia that function with the PDE neuron (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that ZTF-11 is also required for glial fate in the postdeirid lineage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the loss of glial markers.

claim: The number of LIN-32-expressing V5 lineage cells was unchanged in ztf-11 cKO animals.
source: The number of LIN-32-expressing V5 lineage cells was unchanged in ztf-11 cKO animals (Figure 4C–D), indicating that V5 lineage cells still undergo the stereotyped cell divisions that would generate neurons and glia in wild-type animals.
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figures 4C-D.

claim: V5 lineage cells still undergo the stereotyped cell divisions that would generate neurons and glia in wild-type animals in ztf-11 cKO.
source: The number of LIN-32-expressing V5 lineage cells was unchanged in ztf-11 cKO animals (Figure 4C–D), indicating that V5 lineage cells still undergo the stereotyped cell divisions that would generate neurons and glia in wild-type animals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the unchanged number of LIN-32-expressing cells.

claim: lin-32 mutants do not go through postdeirid cell divisions, and instead exclusively adopt epithelial V1-4-like lineages.
source: This is in contrast to lin-32 mutants, which do not go through postdeirid cell divisions, and instead exclusively adopt epithelial V1-4-like lineages (Kenyon, 1986; Zhao and Emmons, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In wild-type animals, the expression of the seam cell fate marker SCM::GFP is invariably lost in lin-32-positive postdeirid cells as they acquire neuronal/glial fate.
source: In wild-type animals, the expression of the seam cell fate marker SCM::GFP is invariably lost in lin-32-positive postdeirid cells as they acquire neuronal/glial fate.
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis.

claim: In ztf-11 cKO animals, some lin-32-positive postdeirid cells retained seam cell fate marker expression.
source: Strikingly, in ztf-11 cKO animals, we observed that some lin-32-positive postdeirid cells retained seam cell fate marker expression (Figure 4D and F), suggesting that ztf-11 was required for the removal of epithelial identity preceding the acquisition of neuronal identity.
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figures 4D and F.

claim: ztf-11 was required for the removal of epithelial identity preceding the acquisition of neuronal identity.
source: Strikingly, in ztf-11 cKO animals, we observed that some lin-32-positive postdeirid cells retained seam cell fate marker expression (Figure 4D and F), suggesting that ztf-11 was required for the removal of epithelial identity preceding the acquisition of neuronal identity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the retention of seam cell markers.

claim: ZTF-11 plays a role in eliminating epithelial fate in differentiating V5 lineage cells.
source: These data are consistent with the notion that ZTF-11 plays a role in eliminating epithelial fate in differentiating V5 lineage cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the retention of epithelial markers in ztf-11 cKO.

claim: In 45% of transgenic animals expressing ZTF-11 in seam cells, additional cells expressing the PVD cell marker were found anterior to the wild-type PVD.
source: Remarkably, we found that ectopic expression of ZTF-11 led to transformation into a neuronal lineage. In 45% of transgenic animals expressing ZTF-11 in seam cells, we found additional cells expressing the PVD cell marker anterior to the wild-type PVD (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from gain-of-function experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ectopic PVD-like cells showed the characteristic 'dendritic menorah' morphology of PVD neurons.
source: In addition, ectopic PVD-like cells showed the characteristic 'dendritic menorah' morphology of PVD neurons (Albeg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: The positions of the ectopic PVDs were consistent with positions of V1-4 seam cell precursors.
source: The positions of the ectopic PVDs were consistent with positions of V1-4 seam cell precursors (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data shown in Figures 5A-B.

claim: Additional PDE-like cells were identified based on the presence of the PDE cell marker and PDE morphology.
source: Similarly, additional PDE-like cells were identified based on the presence of the PDE cell marker and PDE morphology (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression and morphology analysis shown in Figures 5C-D.

claim: Additional glia-like cells could not be identified with ZTF-11 overexpression.
source: In contrast to the proneural activity of ZTF-11, additional glia-like cells could not be identified (Figure 5D), suggesting additional requirements for glia development.
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There are additional requirements for glia development beyond ZTF-11.
source: In contrast to the proneural activity of ZTF-11, additional glia-like cells could not be identified (Figure 5D), suggesting additional requirements for glia development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of ectopic glia.

claim: Some seam cells lost their identity marker when ZTF-11 was ectopically expressed in seam cell lineages.
source: In animals ectopically expressing ZTF-11 in seam cells, we indeed found that some seam cells lost their identity marker (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figures 5E-F.

claim: The loss of seam cell identity resulted in 'gaps' in the seam cell syncytium.
source: Using the apical junction marker AJM-1::GFP, we found that the loss of seam cell identity resulted in 'gaps' in the seam cell syncytium (Figure 5E–F), suggesting that ztf-11 is capable of eliminating epithelial identity and function.
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figures 5E-F.

claim: ztf-11 is capable of eliminating epithelial identity and function.
source: Using the apical junction marker AJM-1::GFP, we found that the loss of seam cell identity resulted in 'gaps' in the seam cell syncytium (Figure 5E–F), suggesting that ztf-11 is capable of eliminating epithelial identity and function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gaps in the seam cell syncytium.

claim: Ectopic PVD-like cells could not be generated by ZTF-11 overexpression in the lin-32(u282) loss of function background.
source: Ectopic PVD-like cells could not be generated by ZTF-11 overexpression in the lin-32(u282) loss of function background (Figure 5B), suggesting that the proneural activity of ZTF-11 depends on proneural bHLH function.
evidence: This is an observation from gain-of-function experiments in a mutant background shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The proneural activity of ZTF-11 depends on proneural bHLH function.
source: Ectopic PVD-like cells could not be generated by ZTF-11 overexpression in the lin-32(u282) loss of function background (Figure 5B), suggesting that the proneural activity of ZTF-11 depends on proneural bHLH function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the requirement for lin-32 in ZTF-11-induced neurogenesis.

claim: The ectopic neurons induced by misexpression of ZTF-11 turned on lin-32 transcriptional reporter, whereas ZTF-11::GFP-positive non-neuronal cells did not.
source: Consistent with the requirement for LIN-32, we found that the ectopic neurons induced by misexpression of ZTF-11 turned on lin-32 transcriptional reporter, whereas ZTF-11::GFP-positive non-neuronal cells did not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that ZTF-11 overexpression can induce expression of LIN-32 to drive neuronal fate.
evidence: This is an observation from reporter expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ZTF-11 overexpression can induce expression of LIN-32 to drive neuronal fate.
source: Consistent with the requirement for LIN-32, we found that the ectopic neurons induced by misexpression of ZTF-11 turned on lin-32 transcriptional reporter, whereas ZTF-11::GFP-positive non-neuronal cells did not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that ZTF-11 overexpression can induce expression of LIN-32 to drive neuronal fate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the activation of lin-32 reporter in ectopic neurons.

claim: ZTF-11 continued to eliminate epithelial identity in the lin-32(u282) mutant.
source: In contrast, we found that ZTF-11 continued to eliminate epithelial identity in the lin-32(u282) mutant (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ZTF-11 can induce LIN-32 to specify neuronal and glial cell fate in certain circumstances.
source: These results indicate that ZTF-11 can induce LIN-32 to specify neuronal and glial cell fate in certain circumstances.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis.

claim: LIN-32 promotes the 'neuronal' features, while ZTF-11 helps to erase epithelial identity from prospective neuronal/glial daughters of the V5 lineage.
source: While LIN-32 promotes the 'neuronal' features, ZTF-11 helps to erase epithelial identity from prospective neuronal/glial daughters of the V5 lineage (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a model summarizing the findings illustrated in Figure 5G.

claim: UNC-86 expression in the respective positions of AVM and PVM nuclei was invariantly lost in ztf-11(tm2315) late L1 animals.
source: We found that UNC-86 expression in the respective positions of AVM and PVM nuclei was invariantly lost in ztf-11(tm2315) late L1 animals (Figure 6B–D), suggesting that ZTF-11 is required for both AVM and PVM postembryonic neuronal fates.
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figures 6B-D.

claim: ZTF-11 is required for both AVM and PVM postembryonic neuronal fates.
source: We found that UNC-86 expression in the respective positions of AVM and PVM nuclei was invariantly lost in ztf-11(tm2315) late L1 animals (Figure 6B–D), suggesting that ZTF-11 is required for both AVM and PVM postembryonic neuronal fates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the loss of UNC-86 expression.

claim: UNC-86 expression was not lost in embryonic neurons such as ALM in ztf-11(tm2315) animals.
source: In contrast, UNC-86 expression was not lost in embryonic neurons such as ALM (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Loss of the respective cell fate markers for RMH (SEM-2) and DVB (LIM-6) was found in ztf-11(tm2315) late L1 animals.
source: We again found loss of the respective cell fate markers for RMH (Figure 6B,E) and DVB (Figure 6B,F), SEM-2 (Vidal et al., 2015) and LIM-6 (Hobert et al., 1999), in ztf-11(tm2315) late L1 animals.
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figures 6B, E, and F.

claim: The aminergic neuron marker CAT-1 was largely lost (89% of animals) in VC4-5 in ztf-11 cKO animals.
source: We found that the aminergic neuron marker CAT-1 was largely lost (89% of animals) in VC4-5, suggesting that ZTF-11 is required for VC4-5 fates.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from marker expression analysis.

claim: ZTF-11 is required for VC4-5 fates.
source: We found that the aminergic neuron marker CAT-1 was largely lost (89% of animals) in VC4-5, suggesting that ZTF-11 is required for VC4-5 fates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the loss of CAT-1 expression.

claim: More subtle decreases in total cholinergic (19%) or GABAergic (5%) VMNs were found in ztf-11 cKO animals.
source: With cholinergic (CHO-1) and GABAergic (UNC-47) neuronal markers, we found more subtle decreases in total cholinergic (19%) or GABAergic (5%) VMNs in ztf-11 cKO animals.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from marker expression analysis.

claim: VC4-5 neurons do not mature until the late L4 stage and maintain expression of ZTF-11 into adulthood.
source: Unlike cholinergic or GABAergic postembryonic VMNs, VC4-5 neurons do not mature until the late L4 stage and maintain expression of ZTF-11 into adulthood (data not shown), which may account for their stronger requirement for ZTF-11.
evidence: This is an observation from expression analysis.

claim: The stronger requirement for ZTF-11 in VC4-5 neurons may be accounted for by their late maturation and maintained ZTF-11 expression.
source: Unlike cholinergic or GABAergic postembryonic VMNs, VC4-5 neurons do not mature until the late L4 stage and maintain expression of ZTF-11 into adulthood (data not shown), which may account for their stronger requirement for ZTF-11.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the stronger requirement.

claim: ZTF-11 functions in multiple neuroectoblast lineages to specify postembryonic neuronal identities.
source: Taken together, our loss-of-function analysis suggest that ZTF-11 functions in multiple neuroectoblast lineages to specify postembryonic neuronal identities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of multiple postembryonic lineages.

claim: Most embryonic neurons are born and obtain neuronal fate in ztf-11 mutants.
source: Using a pan-neuronal RAB-3 marker, we found that most embryonic neurons are born and obtain neuronal fate in ztf-11 mutants (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There was a small (2%) loss of rab-3 expressing nuclei in the ventral cord in ztf-11 mutants.
source: We found that there was a small (2%) loss of rab-3 expressing nuclei in the ventral cord, suggesting that ZTF-11 is mostly dispensable for neuronal fate acquisition during embryogenesis (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ZTF-11 is mostly dispensable for neuronal fate acquisition during embryogenesis.
source: We found that there was a small (2%) loss of rab-3 expressing nuclei in the ventral cord, suggesting that ZTF-11 is mostly dispensable for neuronal fate acquisition during embryogenesis (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the small loss of rab-3 expressing nuclei.

claim: ztf-11(tm2315) homozygote progeny from mothers treated with ztf-11 RNAi still generated a normal number of embryonic VMNs.
source: To account for potential maternal contribution of ZTF-11, we additionally knocked down ZTF-11 in ztf-11(tm2315)/hT2 heterozygote mothers by feeding RNAi and found that their ztf-11(tm2315) homozygote progeny still generated a normal number of embryonic VMNs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an observation from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: No significant changes in cholinergic or glutamatergic head neurons were found in ztf-11(tm2315) mutant animals.
source: With this caveat, we did not find significant changes in cholinergic or glutamatergic head neurons in ztf-11(tm2315) mutant animals, suggesting that ZTF-11 might indeed be dispensable for neuronal fates of major neurotransmitter types.
evidence: This is an observation from marker expression analysis.

claim: ZTF-11 might indeed be dispensable for neuronal fates of major neurotransmitter types during embryogenesis.
source: With this caveat, we did not find significant changes in cholinergic or glutamatergic head neurons in ztf-11(tm2315) mutant animals, suggesting that ZTF-11 might indeed be dispensable for neuronal fates of major neurotransmitter types.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of significant changes in neurotransmitter-specific neurons.

claim: ztf-11 is particularly important for neurons that are generated from epidermal lineages that have fully differentiated in both morphology and function.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that ztf-11 is particularly important for neurons that are generated from epidermal lineages that have fully differentiated in both morphology and function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential requirement for ztf-11 in embryonic vs. postembryonic neurons.

claim: The ztf-11 deletion mutants showed near complete loss of movement.
source: Despite the near normal cell number, the ztf-11 deletion mutants showed near complete loss of movement.
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral analysis.

claim: ztf-11(tm2315) mutant individuals were completely immobile in bacterial lawns after hatching.
source: When maintained with the hT2 balancer chromosome, ztf-11(tm2315) heterozygous mothers produced homozygous mutant individuals that were completely immobile in bacterial lawns after hatching.
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral analysis.

claim: ztf-11(tm2315) mutant individuals invariantly did not develop any further after hatching, potentially due to feeding deficits.
source: ztf-11(tm2315) mutant individuals also invariantly did not develop any further after hatching, potentially due to feeding deficits.
evidence: This is an observation with a speculative explanation.

claim: Homozygous ztf-11(tm2315) mutant individuals showed near complete loss of thrashing motion and severely uncoordinated swimming motion.
source: We found that homozygous ztf-11(tm2315) mutant individuals showed near complete loss of thrashing motion and severely uncoordinated swimming motion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from thrashing assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Heterozygous ztf-11(tm2315)/hT2 individuals did not show a significant change in the number of thrashes compared to wild type (N2).
source: In comparison, heterozygous ztf-11(tm2315)/hT2 individuals did not show a significant change in the number of thrashes compared to wild type (N2) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from thrashing assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ztf-11 may be required for proper function of embryonic neurons.
source: These results raise the possibility that ztf-11 may be required for proper function of embryonic neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the severe behavioral defects despite near-normal neuron numbers.

claim: Proneural genes induce neuronal fate while Notch signaling inhibits neurogenesis by inhibiting proneural genes.
source: Previous studies suggested that proneural genes induce neuronal fate while Notch signaling inhibits neurogenesis by inhibiting proneural genes (Bertrand et al., 2002; Lewis, 1998; Heitzler et al., 1996; Takebayashi et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Myt1 family factors are induced by proneural genes and act as transcriptional repressors of Notch signaling, including the Notch effector gene Hes1.
source: Myt1 family factors are induced by proneural genes and act as transcriptional repressors of Notch signaling, including the Notch effector gene Hes1 (Dhanesh et al., 2016; Mall et al., 2017; Vasconcelos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Repressing Hes1 transcription is thought to de-repress proneural bHLHs such as Ascl1, mediating exit from a proliferative neural stem cell fate and subsequent neuronal differentiation.
source: Repressing Hes1 transcription is in turn thought to de-repress proneural bHLHs such as Ascl1, mediating exit from a proliferative neural stem cell fate and subsequent neuronal differentiation (Mall et al., 2017; Vasconcelos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The C. elegans orthologs of Hes1, lin-22, and its target proneural gene lin-32/Atoh1, function in postdeirid development.
source: The C. elegans orthologs of Hes1, lin-22, and its target proneural gene lin-32/Atoh1, function in postdeirid development (Kenyon, 1986; Portman and Emmons, 2000; Wrischnik and Kenyon, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: lin-22/Hes1 is expressed in seam cells, including V1-4, but not in V5.
source: lin-22/Hes1 is expressed in seam cells, including V1-4, but not in V5 (Katsanos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In lin-32/Atoh1 mutants, no PVD or PDE cells were generated.
source: In lin-32/Atoh1 mutants, no PVD or PDE cells were generated, while in lin-22 mutants, additional PVD and PDE neurons were generated in each of the V1-4 lineages, suggesting that lin-22 represses proneural gene lin-32 in V1-4, but not in the V5 lineage (Portman and Emmons, 2000; Wrischnik and Kenyon, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In lin-22 mutants, additional PVD and PDE neurons were generated in each of the V1-4 lineages.
source: In lin-32/Atoh1 mutants, no PVD or PDE cells were generated, while in lin-22 mutants, additional PVD and PDE neurons were generated in each of the V1-4 lineages, suggesting that lin-22 represses proneural gene lin-32 in V1-4, but not in the V5 lineage (Portman and Emmons, 2000; Wrischnik and Kenyon, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: lin-22 represses proneural gene lin-32 in V1-4, but not in the V5 lineage.
source: In lin-32/Atoh1 mutants, no PVD or PDE cells were generated, while in lin-22 mutants, additional PVD and PDE neurons were generated in each of the V1-4 lineages, suggesting that lin-22 represses proneural gene lin-32 in V1-4, but not in the V5 lineage (Portman and Emmons, 2000; Wrischnik and Kenyon, 1997).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The LIN-22 transcriptional reporter was invariantly excluded from V5 lineage cells during postdeirid development.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we found that the LIN-22 transcriptional reporter was invariantly excluded from V5 lineage cells during postdeirid development (Figure 8B, top panel; Figure 8C).
evidence: This is an observation from reporter expression analysis shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: In the ztf-11 cKO, the LIN-22 reporter remained undetectable in V5 lineages.
source: However, in the ztf-11 cKO, the LIN-22 reporter remained undetectable in V5 lineages.
evidence: This is an observation from reporter expression analysis.

claim: No change in the expression pattern or level of the LIN-22 reporter in V1-4 was detected in ztf-11 cKO.
source: In addition, we detected no change in the expression pattern or level of the LIN-22 reporter in V1-4 (Figure 8B, bottom panel; Figure 8C).
evidence: This is an observation from reporter expression analysis shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: lin-22 is unlikely to be a transcriptional target of ZTF-11.
source: This result suggests that lin-22 is unlikely to be a transcriptional target of ZTF-11.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of change in lin-22 expression.

claim: ztf-11 cKO; lin-22 double mutant resulted in a loss of the PVD cell marker in V1-4 as well as V5 lineages.
source: Contrary to this prediction, we observed that ztf-11 cKO; lin-22 double mutant resulted in a loss of the PVD cell marker in V1-4 as well as V5 lineages (Figure 8D–E).
evidence: This is an observation from genetic epistasis analysis shown in Figures 8D-E.

claim: Both the genetic and expression data argue against the proposed model in which ZTF-11 acts via repression of LIN-22.
source: Both the genetic and expression data argue against the proposed model in which ZTF-11 acts via repression of LIN-22.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and expression data.

claim: lin-32 is still expressed in the V5 lineage at the level of wild-type controls in ztf-11 cKO mutant.
source: To understand ztf-11's relationship with lin-32, we examined lin-32 expression in ztf-11 cKO mutant and found that lin-32 is still expressed in the V5 lineage at the level of wild-type controls (Figure 8F–G).
evidence: This is an observation from reporter expression analysis shown in Figures 8F-G.

claim: ZTF-11 expression in the V5 lineage is completely eliminated in the lin-32 mutant.
source: However, ZTF-11 expression in the V5 lineage is completely eliminated in the lin-32 mutant (Figure 8A), suggesting that ztf-11 is turned on by LIN-32.
evidence: This is an observation from expression analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: ztf-11 is turned on by LIN-32.
source: However, ZTF-11 expression in the V5 lineage is completely eliminated in the lin-32 mutant (Figure 8A), suggesting that ztf-11 is turned on by LIN-32.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the loss of ZTF-11 expression in lin-32 mutants.

claim: The E-box sequences in the promoter region of ztf-11 are required for its expression.
source: This is consistent with the fact that the E-box sequences in the promoter region of ztf-11 are required for its expression (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The loss of lin-32 did not alter the ability of ectopically expressed ZTF-11 to reprogram epithelial identity.
source: Additionally, the loss of lin-32 did not alter the ability of ectopically expressed ZTF-11 to reprogram epithelial identity (Figure 5B), suggesting that ztf-11 acts downstream of both lin-22 and lin-32 to repress epithelial fate.
evidence: This is an observation from gain-of-function experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ztf-11 acts downstream of both lin-22 and lin-32 to repress epithelial fate.
source: Additionally, the loss of lin-32 did not alter the ability of ectopically expressed ZTF-11 to reprogram epithelial identity (Figure 5B), suggesting that ztf-11 acts downstream of both lin-22 and lin-32 to repress epithelial fate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic analysis.

claim: No significant change in fluorescence intensity of lin-32 transcriptional reporter was observed between wild type and ztf-11 cKO during postdeirid development.
source: However, we did not observe a significant change in fluorescence intensity between wild type and ztf-11 cKO.
evidence: This is an observation from reporter expression analysis.

claim: The results argue against the existing model in which ztf-11 acts through repressing lin-22 and instead support a linear genetic model in which lin-22/Hes1 represses lin-32/Atoh1, which in turn activates ztf-11.
source: Together, these results argue against the existing model in which ztf-11 acts through repressing lin-22 and instead support a linear genetic model in which lin-22/Hes1 represses lin-32/Atoh1, which in turn activates ztf-11 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and expression data, illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: ztf-11 transcript levels were reduced by 72% in ztf-11 knockdown embryos.
source: Consistent with this observed reduction of ZTF-11::GFP, we found that ztf-11 transcript levels were reduced by 72% in ztf-11 knockdown embryos (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 419 genes were significantly dysregulated in ztf-11 KD embryos (FDR < 0.1).
source: Differential expression analysis revealed that 419 genes were significantly dysregulated in ztf-11 KD embryos (FDR < 0.1) (Figure 9A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The majority (88%) of the differentially expressed genes were upregulated in ztf-11 KD.
source: The majority (88%) of the differentially expressed genes were upregulated in ztf-11 KD, consistent with the hypothesis that ztf-11 acts a transcriptional repressor (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9A (note: the text says Figure 6A but this appears to be an error).

claim: Among the upregulated genes, the vast majority were non-neuronal genes, including genes specific to epidermis (collagens) or muscle (sarcomere components).
source: Notably, among the upregulated genes, the vast majority were non-neuronal genes, including genes specific to epidermis (collagens) or muscle (sarcomere components) (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is an observation from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: GO-term enrichment analysis revealed that epidermal and muscular genes were significantly enriched among upregulated genes.
source: GO-term enrichment analysis revealed that epidermal and muscular genes were significantly enriched among upregulated genes.
evidence: This is a finding from GO-term enrichment analysis.

claim: No significant changes in expression of most neuronal genes were found in ztf-11 knockdown, including those involved in neurodevelopment, synaptic transmission, axon guidance, and neurotransmitter synthesis.
source: In contrast, we did not find significant changes in expression of most neuronal genes, including those involved in neurodevelopment, synaptic transmission, axon guidance, and neurotransmitter synthesis (Figure 9C), likely reflecting our findings that embryonic neurons are still generated in ztf-11 null mutant.
evidence: This is an observation from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The lack of significant changes in neuronal gene expression likely reflects the finding that embryonic neurons are still generated in ztf-11 null mutant.
source: In contrast, we did not find significant changes in expression of most neuronal genes, including those involved in neurodevelopment, synaptic transmission, axon guidance, and neurotransmitter synthesis (Figure 9C), likely reflecting our findings that embryonic neurons are still generated in ztf-11 null mutant.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-seq and phenotypic data.

claim: The RNA-seq findings are consistent with the genetic analysis, which demonstrated that ZTF-11 acts as a repressor of epithelial identity rather than a direct driver of neuronal fate.
source: These findings are consistent with our genetic analysis, which demonstrated that ZTF-11 acts as a repressor of epithelial identity rather than a direct driver of neuronal fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq and genetic data.

claim: The expression of the transcriptional repressor fusion protein (EnR::ZF) in seam cells resulted in proneural activity similar to overexpression of the native ZTF-11 protein.
source: We found that the expression of the transcriptional repressor fusion protein (EnR::ZF) in seam cells resulted in proneural activity similar to overexpression of the native ZTF-11 protein.
evidence: This is an observation from fusion protein experiments.

claim: Expression of the transcriptional activator fusion protein (VP64::ZF) showed a dominant negative effect and blocked postdeirid neurogenesis.
source: In contrast, expression of the transcriptional activator fusion protein (VP64::ZF) showed a dominant negative effect and blocked postdeirid neurogenesis (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is an observation from fusion protein experiments shown in Figure 10A.

claim: ZTF-11, like vertebrate Myt1 family proteins, functions as a transcriptional repressor to promote neuronal fate.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that ZTF-11, like vertebrate Myt1 family proteins, indeed functions as a transcriptional repressor to promote neuronal fate (Mall et al., 2017; Vasconcelos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fusion protein experiments and comparison to previous research.

claim: In rba-1 or lin-53 single mutants, approximately 20% of the PVD neurons are missing while another 40% of PVDs showed severe morphological defects.
source: In rba-1 or lin-53 single mutants, approximately 20% of the PVD neurons are missing while another 40% of PVDs showed severe morphological defects (Figure 10C–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from mutant analysis shown in Figures 10C-D.

claim: The histone chaperone RbAp46/68 homologs, rba-1 and lin-53, were required for proper postdeirid neurogenesis.
source: This result suggests that the histone chaperone RbAp46/68 homologs, rba-1 and lin-53, were required for proper postdeirid neurogenesis and that ZTF-11 likely functions through a corepressor complex containing histone chaperones RbAp46/48.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mutant phenotypes.

claim: ZTF-11 likely functions through a corepressor complex containing histone chaperones RbAp46/48.
source: This result suggests that the histone chaperone RbAp46/68 homologs, rba-1 and lin-53, were required for proper postdeirid neurogenesis and that ZTF-11 likely functions through a corepressor complex containing histone chaperones RbAp46/48.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mutant phenotypes.

claim: No defects resulting from the loss of sin-3, the sole Sin3 homolog in worms, were observed in postdeirid neurogenesis.
